To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the nuclear receptor coregulators are not only transcriptional coactivators, but also act as coupling proteins during the synthesis and maturation of RNA transcripts.
a subset of nuclear receptor coregulators are required for the synthesis of the RNA primary transcripts and for the maturation of these RNA transcripts in the nucleus.

a subset of nuclear receptor coregulators, including SRC-1, CBP, p300, and PGC-1α, play a key role in the coordination and integration of the steps of gene expression, from transcription to translation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of novel factors involved in the control of gene expression and the elucidation of the mechanisms by which these factors act.
the role of nuclear receptor coregulators in the regulation of gene expression at the nuclear level.
the study of the mechanisms that control gene expression.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the nuclear coregulators act as "coupling proteins" during synthesis and maturation of RNA transcripts.
the coregulator proteins act as coupling proteins during gene expression.

a subset of the transcriptional coregulator proteins are also involved in the maturation and export of RNA transcripts, and thus play a role in coupling the different steps of the gene-expression process.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
transcriptional coregulatory proteins act as coupling proteins that coordinate the synthesis of primary transcripts and their processing to the mature mRNPs that are exported to the cytoplasm.
transcriptional coregulator proteins act as coupling proteins between the different steps of gene expression.
transcriptional coregulator proteins are involved in the synthesis and maturation of RNA transcripts, as well as in their subsequent nuclear export and cytoplasmic translation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the nuclear receptor coregulators are not just passive participants in gene regulation, but they actively contribute to the coordinated regulation of gene expression.
the transcriptional coregulator proteins are involved in the coordination of all the steps of gene expression, including transcription, splicing, capping, polyadenylation, export, and translation.
the same coregulators can control the transcriptional activity of genes and the processing of their transcripts.
